sentences.text: Albertosaurus was a large bipedal predator, though smaller than Tarbosaurus and Tyrannosaurus.
Adults grew up to 8 to 9 meters in length and weighed between 1.7 and 3.0 metric tons.
It possessed long legs ending in a four-toed foot with a very short hallux that did not touch the ground.
Henry Fairfield Osborn named the genus in 1905.
The name honors the Canadian province of Alberta, where the initial remains were found that same year.
The type species is Albertosaurus sarcophagus.
The holotype, the specimen the species is based on, is a partial skull collected on June 9, 1884.
The discovery of 26 Albertosaurus individuals at a single site provides evidence of gregarious behavior.
The presence of an enlarged pneumatic opening in the palatine bone is considered a unique trait that validates Albertosaurus as a distinct taxon.
William Abler demonstrated that teeth with ampullas are structurally stronger, similar to how drilled holes make plexiglass 25% stronger than bars with only regular incisions.
The youngest known Albertosaurus was a two-year-old individual weighing approximately 50 kilograms and measuring slightly more than 2 meters in length.
This animal belongs to the theropod family Tyrannosauridae and the subfamily Albertosaurinae.
Its closest relative is the slightly older Gorgosaurus libratus.
Albertosaurus and Gorgosaurus are the only described species in the subfamily Albertosaurinae, though other undescribed species may exist.
Albertosaurus sarcophagus has synonyms including Deinodon sarcophagus and Albertosaurus arctunguis.
Albertosaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically from the latest Campanian to the early Maastrichtian stages.
It lived approximately 71 million years ago.
The animal inhabited northwestern North America.
Most Albertosaurus sarcophagus fossils come from the upper Horseshoe Canyon Formation in Alberta, dating to the early Maastrichtian (70 to 68 million years ago).
There is a scientific debate regarding the genus content of Albertosaurus, with some researchers recognizing Gorgosaurus libratus as a distinct species.
Fossils reported from Montana, New Mexico, Wyoming, and Missouri are debated; they may not belong to Albertosaurus sarcophagus or the genus Albertosaurus at all.

There is a debate among authors regarding whether Albertosaurus and Gorgosaurus should remain separate genera, with most following Philip J. Currie's recommendation to keep them separate but some disagreeing.
It is debated whether Albertosaurus sternbergi is a juvenile Gorgosaurus libratus, identical to Tyrannosaurus, or a separate genus named Nanotyrannus.
